Photograph: Ethan Swope/AP California Sinkhole at Malibu home reportedly owned by Nicolas Cage prompts evacuation More than 30 properties ordered to evacuate after sinkhole grows to roughly 25-30ft deep and 30 by 60 feet wide Anna Betts Wed 9 Sep 2026 09.53 EDT Last modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 10.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The city of Malibu, California, has ordered the evacuation of more than 30 properties after a large sinkhole opened on Tuesday. Malibu officials declared a local emergency on Tuesday evening after a “large sinkhole” emerged near 31630 Sea Level Drive. The officials said the sinkhole was believed to have begun developing on Monday, and had grown to roughly 25-30ft deep and 30 by 60ft wide by Tuesday evening. In an earlier update on Tuesday, officials said they were responding to the “collapse of a driveway” and a resulting gas leak, which had been reported at about 5.45am local time. The Los Angeles county sheriff’s department and Los Angeles county fire department closed the private road and identified the gas leak. Actor Nicolas Cage is reportedly the owner of the home where the sinkhole formed. Cage purchased the home in 2024, the New York Times noted . A representative for Cage did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “Conditions are continuing to be evaluated, and the full extent of the impacts is not yet known,” Malibu city officials said on Tuesday evening, warning that the sinkhole “poses imminent danger to the homes and residents along Sea Level Drive”. By Tuesday evening, 31 properties were under an evacuation order. Officials said that seven homes had been red-tagged because of “hazardous conditions resulting from the sinkhole” while another 24 residences were red-tagged “due to the loss of safe vehicular access”. Sheriff’s deputies notified residents in person and a digital alert had been issued. Gas service to the affected area was shut off by Tuesday evening and city officials warned that water service “may also be discontinued as conditions warrant”. They also cautioned that “conditions are likely to worsen with forecasted high tides and rains”. Additionally, Post-tropical Cyclone Marie could continue to bring “increased rainfall and high surf” to the area. The National Weather Service said on Tuesday that “swells generated by Marie will continue to affect portions of the coast of the Baja California Peninsula and southern California for the next couple of days”. A coastal flood advisory had been in effect until 11pm local time on Tuesday, Malibu officials said. A temporary shelter was also established by the American Red Cross at Malibu high school. City officials said that emergency personnel access “is severely constrained and may be impassable, due to the large portion of the road that has collapsed”. They said that as of Tuesday evening, the “intact portion of the roadway is too narrow to accommodate emergency response vehicles, including fire engines and other large apparatus, creating a substantial risk to public safety and emergency response capabilities”. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/15/un-u.text: The United Nations has called on Israel to grant international investigators access to every part of Gaza, as the recovery of human remains from the territory's ruins continues nearly three years after the war began.The UN's human rights office said gathering evidence at destroyed sites was essential, urging that "international investigators be allowed into all parts of Gaza to assist with evidence-gathering."Most of the dead being recovered are reported to be women and children, a detail the UN says points to the likelihood that war crimes were committed during the campaign."The remains of what appears to be entire families are now being unearthed at locations that were pulverised by Israeli attacks," UN rights chief Volker Turk pointed out in a statement."I worry the remains recovered so far may only be the tip of the iceberg," he said, pointing to how "much of Gaza has been flattened by Israeli bombing or demolition and clearing by heavy machinery and explosives"."Today, many areas in Gaza where the Israeli military is deployed continue to be levelled by bulldozers with no respect for the dead under the rubble," he said.According to the Palestinian Civil Defence, more than 630 bodies and other remains have been pulled from beneath collapsed buildings across Gaza since last November alone.The UN's rights office cited an estimate that over 8,000 people remain missing under the rubble — a figure that underscores how much of the territory's devastation has yet to be fully accounted for.Turk insisted that "every feasible effort must be taken to document and identify these victims, preserve forensic information and biological samples, record their burial locations and inform their families"."The discovery of extensive remains under the rubble in Gaza City resurfaces (the) concerns of war crimes and other atrocity crimes," he warned.The war began after Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, which killed at least 1,195 people according to official Israeli data. Israel's subsequent bombing campaign and ground invasion left much of Gaza in ruins.Gaza's health ministry, which operates under Hamas authority, says the offensive has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians in total, including over 1,350 since a ceasefire was signed last October.For European governments navigating the diplomatic fallout of the conflict, the UN's call adds pressure on Israel to open Gaza to independent scrutiny at a moment when the scale of civilian loss is still being uncovered.

Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty Images West Bank UN adds 61 firms to settlements blacklist over alleged human rights violations against Palestinians Israel ‘categorically rejects’ publication and says businesses on database have committed no wrongdoing Associated Press Sat 26 Sep 2026 07.10 EDT Last modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 07.42 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The UN human rights office has added 61 more companies to a blacklist of firms that it says are involved in violating Palestinian human rights through business ties to Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank . The vast majority of the total 214 companies, which are based in 11 countries, are Israeli. Five of the 158 companies listed last year were removed in the latest update. The blacklist, first published in 2020, was born of a vote by the UN’s human rights council, which has no ability to force companies to act. Its main goal is to name and shame businesses with ties to the settlements. It is unclear how the inclusion on the list has affected the companies financially. “This report is another reminder to companies that they have human rights responsibilities and are expected to conduct due diligence to ensure that they do not become involved in human rights violations or abuses,” said Volker Türk, the UN human rights chief, in a statement. Israel said it “categorically rejects” the publication. “This database is meant to serve as a blacklist against businesses that have committed no wrongdoing,” the Israeli diplomatic mission in Geneva said in a statement. “We call on friends not to yield to this ugly attempt to blacklist Israeli firms.” The UN office said it had advised the companies of their listing and given them a right of reply. The latest report comes as Israeli settlements in Palestinian areas have faced new scrutiny. Earlier this month, Britain banned trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, where it says “settler terrorists” are carrying out “ethnic cleansing” of Palestinians. France and Canada announced they would take similar action. https://www.thedickinsonpress.com/opinio.text: ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Commentary: Economic populism is a dead end for the GOP Modern Republicans are increasingly embracing economic demagoguery and doomerism David Harsanyi is a national columnist. Contributed By David Harsanyi September 20, 2026 at 6:51 AM Listen Comments Share Share this article Opinion Opinion Advocates for ideas and draws conclusions based on the interpretation of facts and data. The Trust Project What is this? It was probably inevitable that the Right's economic populism would degenerate into promises of more government checks. Early last week, the administration floated the idea of redirecting federal childcare aid so low-income married stay-at-home parents could get a $9,000 subsidy per child for daycare. ADVERTISEMENT The policy, reportedly hatched by Vice President JD Vance, would use the Department of Health and Human Services' Child Care and Development Fund, originally created in the 1990s for low-income single parents. Vance's defenders stress that the program merely redirects "existing subsidies" and wouldn't add to the debt. The notion that Vance was fiscally responsible was quickly shattered later in the week when he appeared on television defending President Donald Trump's promise to hand every adult a $5,000 "dividend" check should Republicans hold on to Congress. "We're taking in an extraordinary amount of revenue," Vance told Fox News' Bret Baier. "What the president is saying is, 'If you keep it going, if you keep us in power and allow us to continue to do these things, then you're going to share in some of the benefit of this incredible wealth that we are creating in the United States of America.'" None of this is true. Import taxes on Americans don't create any wealth — they extract it. The administration collected roughly $300 billion from American consumers through tariffs last year. The "revenue" was supposedly going to be used to pay down the debt. Handing out roughly $1.3 trillion to voters, while running an existing $2 trillion deficit, isn't a "dividend" payment as much as a brazen socialistic redistribution stunt that would add $1 trillion to the deficit. Of course, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's contention that the proposal was an "insult" to voters and democracy itself is risible considering that socialistic redistribution is the foundation of the Democratic Party's entire economic agenda these days. More than anything, Schumer was likely perturbed that Republicans were stealing the Left's strategy. And that's the real problem. Republicans are altering the electorate's expectations by conceding core arguments to the Left. Vance's fans argue that welfare programs will never be unwound, so they might as well be used for social conservative goals. Once you normalize arguments in favor of dependency, politics devolves into an arms race in who can send voters bigger checks. Vance's defenders present themselves as champions of stay-at-home mothers and his critics as anti-family, Chamber-of-commerce types, who want to push mothers into the workforce to lift the GDP and destroy nuclear families. That's not the choice. The preexisting program, the CCDF, funds daycares so that already poor single mothers, some of whom have been abandoned or widowed, can go to work and hopefully become self-sufficient. The program was meant to wean people off dependency. ADVERTISEMENT Since the Great Society was hatched, conservatives have argued that welfare throws people into a corrosive generational spiral. Now, you can argue that the CCDF failed at its intended goal, but Vance's plan hooks an entire new group, low-income married mothers, on state funding and incentivizes breadwinners to stay poor enough not to lose the subsidy. There would be a good chance the idea ends up hooking others. Every welfare program that has ever existed is prone to grow bigger. There are many more poor married couples with children than single mothers. The eligibility pool will be far larger. The demand will be far greater. Some fans of the program are already arguing to expand it. The funding for safety net programs is diverted from middle-class families, who don't always have the luxury of a spouse staying home with the children, either. At some point, they'll say, "What about us?" What will populists tell them? And, judging from the wide range of progressive leftist economics embraced by Vance and other economic statists, this might well be the goal. In essence, the argument is that the welfare state can do good things if only it were deployed for the right reasons by the right people. There is little evidence for this, either. Countries such as Hungary have spent chunks of their GDP enticing people to form families, including tax exemptions, cash handouts to mothers, and subsidized loans. This wasn't even aimed at the poor, but at everyone. After a small initial bump in replacement rate, Hungary's fell to an all-time low. Trump's $5,000 check is a gimmick, of course. But Vance's central economic goal is to move the Republican Party away from Reaganism and toward right-progressivism. ADVERTISEMENT Modern Republicans are increasingly embracing economic demagoguery and doomerism. In the end, though, they will never be able to outspend or outpromise the Left. The right-populists' mantra seems to be "fund the family," when it should be "free the family." David Harsanyi is a national columnist. Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/Reuters View image in fullscreen Nearly a million Palestinians have been displaced by the Israeli bombardment, which has killed nearly 75,000 people. Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/Reuters Middle East and north Africa ‘Gaza’s suffering has become campaign fodder’: Palestinians fear the worst from Israel election Humanitarian catastrophe largely ignored as rivals Gadi Eisenkot and Benjamin Netanyahu vow to end Hamas rule Seham Tantesh in Gaza and Lorenzo Tondo Sun 25 Oct 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 02.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google As Israel prepares to go to the polls , Palestinians in Gaza are bracing for an outcome that could shape their future, knowing their fate rests with the country that has reduced much of the territory to rubble and killed nearly 75,000 people. Gaza, where nearly a million displaced Palestinians face dire sanitary conditions, water shortages and the constant threat of Israeli strikes, has been largely absent from the election campaign . Both Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition and Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition Yashar party have focused instead on the goal of destroying Hamas in the wake of the 7 October attacks and the trauma inflicted on Israeli society. The humanitarian catastrophe unfolding just across the border has received little, if any, attention. “We hope a government will come to power that is less inclined towards killing, displacement and our extermination,” said Sami Abu Rumi, 47, from Rafah, who is now displaced in al-Mawasi, Khan Younis. “But, ultimately, we see the thinking of Israeli governments as largely similar.” View image in fullscreen Gadi Eisenkot championed the “Dahiya doctrine” in the 2006 war with Hezbollah, which advocated overwhelming force against civilian areas where militants operated. Photograph: Ariel Schalit/AP Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has set out a clear plan for Gaza’s future . Both have vowed to end Hamas rule and both support Donald Trump’s controversial peace plan. Eisenkot, the former military chief whose party is leading Netanyahu’s Likud in the polls, has pledged to restore Israel’s international standing after three years of war. Yet he is no dove. A senior commander during Israel’s 2006 war with Hezbollah, Eisenkot, whose son and two nephews were killed fighting in Gaza, later championed the “Dahiya doctrine” , which advocated overwhelming force against civilian areas where militants operated. Critics say the strategy has since been employed in Gaza, causing widespread destruction that, they argue, amounts to war crimes. “Eisenkot talks of defeating Hamas , while Netanyahu boasts about military operations and the killing of Palestinians,” said Abu Rumi. ‘‘Gaza’s suffering has become campaign fodder. Meanwhile, families here struggle to feed their children, keep them in school and access medical care. With homes and infrastructure destroyed, simply surviving has become a daily struggle.” Earlier this week, the Arab-led Joint List party in Israel aired a 48-second election video showing drone footage of Gaza’s ruins. “[We] behave as if everything that has happened here is completely normal,” the voiceover says. “As if tens of thousands of people weren’t killed here … as if entire cities were not destroyed and turned into wastelands.” The party vows it “will not be silent”, adding: “[The other parties] want more destruction. We offer life.” ‘The biggest motivation is fear’: High turnout among Israel’s Palestinians could unseat Netanyahu Read more The chances of Arab parties joining an Eisenkot-led coalition are slim to none, although they could offer support from outside government. Yet among Palestinians in Gaza , pessimism runs deep: whoever wins, little is expected to change. “I do not believe anyone genuinely cares about Gaza or has its people’s interests at heart,’’ said Haneen Hamdouna, 45, from Beit Lahia, who has also been displaced to al-Mawasi. ‘‘Whether it is Netanyahu, Eisenkot or someone else, attacking Gaza seems to have become part of Israeli election campaigning. “For years, we have said that the incoming government might be better than the one before it, only to be shocked when it turns out to be worse. Perhaps 200 trucks would be allowed into Gaza instead of 100, but that would not mean any real change in our lives.” In Gaza, most people are too preoccupied by the struggle to find food and water to follow the election campaign. Fears of renewed hunger are mounting as markets run short of fresh produce and other essentials. Residents say commercial deliveries have been suspended for about a week, driving up prices. Flour now costs more than three times its previous price, while dwindling humanitarian aid has left families increasingly vulnerable to another food crisis. View image in fullscreen Candidates in the upcoming Israeli election include Yair Golan of the Democrats party (left billboard) and the Arab-led Joint List. Photograph: Amir Cohen/Reuters Yet, some people in Gaza are following the Israeli elections closely, driven less by hope of change than fear of what the outcome could mean for their future. They fear that Palestinian suffering has become a recurring feature of Israeli election campaigns, with candidates competing over who can take the toughest stance towards Gaza rather than offering any prospect of a better future. “A friend was supposed to hold his son’s wedding in the coming days,” said Karim Mareesh, 43. “But he decided to postpone it until after the Israeli elections. He feared that the far-right government might secure another term, prompting the war to resume and forcing him to flee again. He could lose his tent and the wedding supplies he had struggled to save up for.” Hope is hard to find in Gaza, where three years of war have reduced entire neighbourhoods to wastelands of shattered concrete and bomb craters. It is harder still to imagine a future when Israeli restrictions on food and humanitarian aid have turned hunger into a weapon of war . And almost impossible to see any light at the end of the tunnel when more than 20,000 Palestinian children have been killed since 7 October 2023. “I feel that everything said about addressing our suffering is nothing more than an attempt to soothe our pain, or simply words and promises that we no longer believe,” says Noor AlMoghanni, 20, from Gaza City. “Whether Netanyahu wins or loses, the reality here will not change.
